Cabbage and Ribs | founded = {{Start date and age|df=yes|1875|8|6}} | ground = [[Easter Road]], [[Edinburgh]] | capacity = {{SPFL-stadiums|hibernian}} | owner = Bydand Sports{{cite web|title=THE HIBERNIAN FOOTBALL CLUB LIMITED|url=https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/SC005323/charges|access-date=6 October 2023|website=Gov.UK|archive-date=7 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007123159/https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/SC005323/charges|url-status=live}} | chairman = Ian Gordon | manager = [[Marink Reedijk]] | mgrtitle = Head coach | league = {{Scottish football updater|Hibernia}} | season = {{Scottish football updater|Hibernia2}} | position = {{Scottish football updater|Hibernia3}} | website = {{URL|http://www.hibernianfc.co.uk/}} | pattern_la1 = _hibernian2627h | pattern_b1 = _hibernian2627h | pattern_ra1 = _hibernian2627h | pattern_sh1 = _hibernian2627h | pattern_so1 = _hibernian2627hl | leftarm1 = ffffff | body1 = 335649 | rightarm1 = fffff | shorts1 = ffffff | socks1 = ffffff | pattern_la2 = _hibernian2627a | pattern_b2 = _hibernian2627a | pattern_ra2 = _hibernian2627a | pattern_sh2 = _hibernian2627a | pattern_so2 = _hibernian2627al | leftarm2 = f0ece5 | body2 = f0ece5 | rightarm2 = f0ece5 | shorts2 = 335649 | socks2 = f0ece5 | pattern_la3 = _hibernian2627t | pattern_b3 = _hibernian2627t | pattern_ra3 = _hibernian2627t | pattern_sh3 = _hibernian2627t | pattern_so3 = _hibernian2627tl | leftarm3 = 9d87bf | body3 = 9d87bf | rightarm3 = 9d87bf | shorts3 = 000000 | socks3 = 000000 | current = 2026–27 Hibernian F.C. season }} '''Hibernian Football Club''', commonly known as '''Hibs''' or '''the Hibees''', is a professional [[association football|football]] club based in the [[Leith]] area of [[Edinburgh]], Scotland. The club competes in the [[Scottish Premiership]], the highest division of [[Scottish football]]. Founded in 1875 by members of Edinburgh's Irish community, the club takes its name from ''[[Hibernia]]'', the Latin name for Ireland.{{cite web |title=Our History |url=https://www.hibernianfc.co.uk/club/history/our-history |website=Hibernian FC |access-date=28 October 2026}} Hibernian traditionally play in green shirts with white sleeves and have played their home matches at [[Easter Road]] since 1893. The stadium has a capacity of 20,421. Hibernian became the first British club to compete in the [[European Cup]], reaching the semi-final of the inaugural [[1955–56 European Cup|1955–56 competition]].{{cite news |last=Spurling |first=Jon |title=How Hibs became the first British club to play in the European Cup |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2018/jan/08/hibernian-british-team-european-cup-hibs |work=The Guardian |date=8 January 2018 |access-date=28 October 2026}} The club also reached the semi-final of the [[1960–61 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup]], eliminating [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]] in the quarter-final.{{cite web |title=European Champions' Cup and Fairs' Cup 1960-61 - Details |url=https://www.rsssf.org/ec/ec196061det.html |website=RSSSF |access-date=28 October 2026}} Other notable European victories include those against [[FC Porto|Porto]] and [[Sporting CP]].{{cite web |title=European Champions' Cup and Fairs' Cup 1967-68 - Details |url=https://www.rsssf.org/ec/ec196768det.html |website=RSSSF |access-date=28 October 2026}}{{cite web |title=European Competitions 1972-73 |url=https://www.rsssf.org/ec/ec197273.html |website=RSSSF |access-date=28 October 2026}} In 1967, Hibs overturned a 4–1 first-leg defeat against [[SSC Napoli|Napoli]], scoring five goals past future World Cup winning goalkeeper [[Dino Zoff]] at Easter Road to progress 6–4 on aggregate.{{cite news |title=On This Day: Hibs 5-0 Napoli |url=https://football-italia.net/on-this-day-hibs-5-0-napoli/ |work=Football Italia |date=29 November 2017 |access-date=28 October 2026}} Domestically, Hibernian have won four [[Scottish football champions|Scottish league championships]], three [[Scottish Cup]]s and three [[Scottish League Cup]]s. The club's most successful era came between 1948 and 1952, when Hibs won three league championships during the era of the celebrated [[The Famous Five (football)|Famous Five]] forward line. In 2016, the club ended a 114-year wait to win the Scottish Cup, defeating [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] 3–2 in the [[2016 Scottish Cup final|final]].{{cite news |last=Wilson |first=Richard |title=Scottish Cup final: Rangers 2-3 Hibernian |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/36292302 |work=BBC Sport |date=21 May 2016 |access-date=28 October 2026}} Hibernian's history includes several notable football firsts. On 7 May 1881, the club's former ground, [[Hibernian Park]], hosted the world's first recorded women's international football match, in which Scotland defeated England 3–0.{{cite web |title=Hibernian Women, 1881–2026 |url=https://scottishfootballhistory.scot/clubs/hibernian/hibernian-women/ |website=Scottish Football History |access-date=28 October 2026}}{{cite web |title=The Scottish Women's Football Team 1881 |url=https://www.scottishfootballmuseum.org.uk/exhibitions/hall-of-fame/the-scottish-womens-football-team-1881/ |website=Scottish Football Museum |access-date=28 October 2026}} The club became the first British top-flight team to display a shirt sponsor in 1977.{{cite web |title=A History of Football Kit Design in England and Scotland, Part 7 |url=https://www.historicalkits.co.uk/Articles/History/part-7.html |website=Historical Football Kits |access-date=28 October 2026}} Hibs also pioneered stadium innovations at [[Easter Road]], installing Scotland's first major floodlighting system in 1954 and becoming the first Scottish club to introduce [[undersoil heating]] in 1980.{{cite web |title=Easter Road |url=https://stadiumdb.com/stadiums/sco/easter_road_stadium |website=StadiumDB |access-date=28 October 2026}} The club's fans are renowned for their renditions of ''[[Sunshine on Leith (song)|Sunshine on Leith]]'', a song by Scottish duo [[the Proclaimers]], which is widely acclaimed as one of the greatest anthems in world football.{{cite news |last=McNally |first=Frank |title=Hibernian Rhapsody: Frank McNally on the rise of a great football anthem, Sunshine on Leith |url=https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/an-irish-diary/2026/01/02/hibernian-rhapsody-frank-mcnally-on-the-rise-of-a-great-football-anthem-sunshine-on-leith/ |work=The Irish Times |date=2 January 2026 |access-date=28 October 2026}} It won [[BBC Radio 6 Music|BBC Radio 6 Music’s]] Football Anthems World Cup in 2018, being voted the UK's favourite football anthem.{{cite news |title=Sunshine on Leith voted UK's favourite football anthem |url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/arts-and-culture/sunshine-on-leith-voted-uks-favourite-football-anthem-279507 |work=Edinburgh Evening News |date=28 February 2019 |access-date=28 October 2026}} Hibernian have a longstanding rivalry with [[Heart of Midlothian F.C.|Heart of Midlothian]], with whom they contest the [[Edinburgh derby]]. ==History== {{Main|History of Hibernian F.C.}} {{See also|List of Hibernian F.C. seasons}} ===Foundation and early history (1875–1939)=== [[File:Cowgate, Edinburgh.JPG|thumb|upright|The [[Cowgate]], where Hibs were formed in 1875.]] The club was founded in 1875 by Irishmen living in the [[Cowgate]] area of [[Edinburgh]].{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/articles/2BJKzyV3GpSD66swPg6Gr4h/the-football-team-formed-in-the-shadow-of-famine-that-fought-xenophobia-and-raised-money-for-impoverished-immigrants |title=The football team, formed in the shadow of famine, that fought xenophobia and raised money for impoverished immigrants |publisher=BBC |date=21 November 2018 |access-date=22 November 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181122202312/http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/articles/2BJKzyV3GpSD66swPg6Gr4h/the-football-team-formed-in-the-shadow-of-famine-that-fought-xenophobia-and-raised-money-for-impoverished-immigrants |archive-date=22 November 2018 |url-status=live }} The name ''Hibernian'' (deriving from [[Hibernia]], an ancient name for Ireland{{cite web|url=http://www.hibernianfc.co.uk/page/TimelineDetail/0,,10290~1750533,00.html|title=The Origins of Hibernian – 3|date=11 August 2009|publisher=Hibernian F.C.|work=Hibernianfc.co.uk|access-date=22 February 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716054950/http://www.hibernianfc.co.uk/page/TimelineDetail/0,,10290~1750533,00.html|archive-date=16 July 2011|df=dmy-all}}), the colour green, the [[Celtic harp]] and the [[Irish language]] phrase ''[[Erin go bragh]]'' (meaning ''Ireland Forever'') were adopted as symbols early on.{{cite web |url=http://www.hibernianfc.co.uk/page/TimelineDetail/0,,10290~1750533,00.html |title=Erin go Bragh |publisher=Hibernian F.C. |access-date=15 January 2011 |date=11 August 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716054950/http://www.hibernianfc.co.uk/page/TimelineDetail/0%2C%2C10290~1750533%2C00.html |archive-date=16 July 2011 }} Founder Fr. [[Edward Joseph Hannan]] was the first president of the club and Michael Whelahan its first team captain.{{cite news |url=https://www.limerickleader.ie/news/sport/643568/the-ballingarry-priest-who-founded-famed-scottish-club-hibernian-fc.html |title=The Ballingarry priest who founded famed Scottish club Hibernian FC |first=Mike |last=Hennessey |newspaper=Limerick Leader |date=24 June 2021 |accessdate=9 June 2022 |archive-date=25 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220725181442/https://www.limerickleader.ie/news/sport/643568/the-ballingarry-priest-who-founded-famed-scottish-club-hibernian-fc.html |url-status=live }} [[James Connolly]], the famous [[Socialism|socialist]] and [[Irish republicanism|Irish Republican]] leader, was a Hibs fan,{{Cite news |last=Hannan |first=Martin |url=https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/whose-grass-roots-are-the-greener-1-1288245 |title=Whose grass-roots are the greener? |newspaper=Scotland on Sunday |publisher=Johnston Press |date=20 May 2001 |access-date=9 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160104204806/http://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/whose-grass-roots-are-the-greener-1-1288245 |archive-date=4 January 2016 |url-status=live }}{{Cite news |last=Vallely |first=Joanna |url=http://sport.scotsman.com/hibernianfc/God-squad-signs-up-to.2798179.jp |title=God squad signs up to play host to Hibs past |work=Edinburgh Evening News |publisher=Johnston Press |date=4 August 2006 |access-date=22 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081226002539/http://sport.scotsman.com/hibernianfc/God-squad-signs-up-to.2798179.jp |archive-date=26 December 2008 |url-status=live }} while the club were "closely identified" with the [[Irish Home Rule movement]] during the 1880s. There was some [[Sectarianism|sectarian]] resistance initially to an Irish club participating in [[Football in Scotland|Scottish football]], but Hibs established themselves as a force in Scottish football in the 1880s.{{harvnb|Crampsey|1990|p=27}} Hibs were the first club from the east coast of Scotland to win a major trophy, the [[1886–87 Scottish Cup|1887 Scottish Cup]]. They went on to defeat [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]], who had reached the semi-finals of the [[1886–87 FA Cup|1887 FA Cup]], in a [[Exhibition game|friendly match]] described as the ''[[Football World Championship|Association Football Championship of the World Decider]]''.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jqnq0hIia0cC&q=hibernian+easter+road&pg=PA145|title=Day of the Match: A History of Football in 365 Days|publisher=Boxtree|year=2008|quote=In August 1887, [[Scottish Cup]] holders Hibernian took on [[FA Cup]] winners [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]] in a [[Exhibition game|friendly]] at Hibs' [[Hibernian Park|Easter Road]] ground. Posters appeared all over [[Edinburgh]] billing the encounter as 'The Association Football Championship of the World'. Hibernian won the match 2–1 and therefore had the right (whichever way you look at it, as nobody else had bothered to stage such an event) to call themselves the first world champions, beating [[Uruguay national football team|Uruguay]] to it by 43 years.|author=Scott Murray and Rowan Walker|access-date=17 August 2010|isbn=978-0-7522-2678-1}}{{harvnb|Mackay|1986|p=40}}{{harvnb|Lugton|1999|p=121}} Despite advertising the match as 'The Association Football Championship of the World', Preston had lost in the FA Cup semi-finals to West Bromwich Albion and were not the 'best' English side that year. Mismanagement over the next few years led to Hibs becoming homeless and the club temporarily ceased operating in 1891. A lease on the [[Easter Road]] site was acquired in late 1892 and Hibs played its first match at Easter Road on 4 February 1893.{{Cite web|url=http://www.hibernianfc.co.uk/page/TimelineDetail/0,,10290~1750639,00.html|title=The Origins of Hibernian – Part 12|date=11 August 2009|publisher=Hibernian F.C.|work=Hibernianfc.co.uk|access-date=22 February 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090927103314/http://www.hibernianfc.co.uk/page/TimelineDetail/0,,10290~1750639,00.html|archive-date=27 September 2009|df=dmy-all}} Despite this interruption, the club today views the period since 1875 as one continued history and therefore counts the honours won between 1875 and 1891, including the 1887 Scottish Cup. The club were admitted to the [[Scottish Football League]] in 1893, although they had to win the Second Division twice before being elected into the First Division in 1895. [[File:Hibernian FC 1903.jpg|left|thumb|The Hibs team of 1903]] A significant change at this time was that players were no longer required to be members of the Catholic Young Men's Society.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7YVCwNJW1A8C&q=hibernian+edinburgh+catholic&pg=PA339 |author=Stephen Dobson and John A. Goddard |title=The Economics of Football |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2001 |access-date=16 August 2010 |isbn=978-0-521-66158-4 |quote=Edinburgh Hibernians were founded as the first [[Roman Catholic|catholic]] club in 1875. In its first incarnation, only catholics were permitted to play for Hibernian, but when the club was reconstituted in 1893 the ban on protestants was lifted.}} Hibs are seen today as being an Irish or [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]] institution, as it was in the early years of its history.{{Cite journal|last=Kelly |first=John |title=Hibernian Football Club: The Forgotten Irish? |journal=Sport in Society |date = May 2007|volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=514–536 |doi=10.1080/17430430701333950 |s2cid=143084869 }}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2nMObKWGCVwC&q=hibernian+edinburgh+catholic&pg=PA195|title=The Jambo Experience: An Anthropological Study of Hearts Fans|publisher=Berg|year=1997|quote=Even though Hibs were founded by Irish–Catholic immigrants, this connection to their sectarian origins has faded significantly in the Protestant-dominated Edinburgh of the twentieth century.|author=Hans Kristian Hognestad|isbn=978-1-85973-193-2|access-date=17 August 2010}} For instance, the [[Celtic harp|Irish harp]] was only re-introduced to the club badge when it was last re-designed in 2000. This design reflects the three pillars of the club's identity: Ireland, Edinburgh (the [[Edinburgh Castle|castle]]) and [[Leith]] (the ship). Geography as well as ethnicity and religion shapes the modern fan base of the club, with Hibs drawing most of their support from the north and east of Edinburgh.{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/edinburghcultura0000camp |url-access=registration |page=[https://archive.org/details/edinburghcultura0000camp/page/132 132] |author=Donald Campbell |quote=Sectarian bigotry may not be completely absent from this relationship, but it has always been less important than identification with territory. Hibs supporters tend to belong to the north and east of Edinburgh, while [[Heart of Midlothian F.C.|Hearts]] supporters (who outnumber their city rivals by a ratio of approximately two to one) are more usually found in the south and west. |title=Edinburgh: a Cultural and Literary History |isbn =978-1-902669-73-1 |year=2003 |access-date=16 August 2010 |publisher=Signal Books}}{{Cite news|author-link=Graham Spiers |last=Spiers |first=Graham |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/scotland/article2797038.ece |title=Edinburgh derby is the jewel of game in Scotland |work=The Times|publisher=News International |date=3 November 2007 |access-date=4 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110811235342/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/scotland/article2797038.ece |archive-date=11 August 2011}}{{Cite web |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/rugby_union/scottish/3148651.stm |title=New capital groundshare plan |publisher=BBC Sport |date=13 August 2003 |access-date=22 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031011080259/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/rugby_union/scottish/3148651.stm |archive-date=11 October 2003 |url-status=live }} Hibs had some success after being reformed, winning the [[1901–02 Scottish Cup|1902 Scottish Cup]] and their first [[List of Scottish football champions|league championship]] a year later. After this, however, the club endured a long barren spell. The club lost its placing in the league and were [[promotion and relegation|relegated]] for the first time in 1931, although they were promoted back to the top division two years later. The notorious Scottish Cup drought{{Cite news |last=Black |first=Jim |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/feb/03/newsstory.hibernian |title=Hibs' Cup of woe adds to strife of Reilly |work=[[The Observer]] |date=3 February 2008 |access-date=22 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080416212524/http://football.guardian.co.uk/News_Story/0,,2251647,00.html |archive-date=16 April 2008 |url-status=live }} began as they reached three cup finals, two in consecutive years, but lost each of them. ===The Famous Five (1939–1959)=== [[File:Famous Five mural.JPG|thumb|upright|Picture depicting [[The Famous Five (football)|the Famous Five]] at [[Easter Road]] stadium.|left]] Hibs' most successful era was in the decade following the end of the [[World War II|Second World War]], when it was "among the foremost clubs in Britain". The [[forward (association football)|forward]] line of [[Gordon Smith (footballer, born 1924)|Gordon Smith]], [[Bobby Johnstone]], [[Lawrie Reilly]], [[Eddie Turnbull]] and [[Willie Ormond]], collectively known as [[The Famous Five (football)|the Famous Five]], was "regarded as the finest ever seen in Scottish football".{{Cite web|last=Gordon |first=Phil |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/bobby-johnstone-729354.html |title=Bobby Johnstone |work=The Independent|date=24 August 2001 |access-date=22 February 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081226005513/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/bobby-johnstone-729354.html |archive-date=26 December 2008}} Each of the Famous Five scored more than 100 goals for Hibs. The north stand at [[Easter Road]] is now named in their honour. Smith was signed by Hibs in 1941, while Ormond, Turnbull, Reilly and Johnstone were all signed during 1946. Of the five, only Ormond cost Hibs a transfer fee, [[Pound sterling|£]]1200 from [[Stenhousemuir F.C.|Stenhousemuir]].{{harvnb|Jeffrey|2005|p=125}} Reilly, Johnstone, Smith and Turnbull were all signed from youth or junior leagues. In the first season of competitive football after the Second World War, Hibs reached the [[1947 Scottish Cup final]]. They took an early lead in the match, but went on to lose 2–1 to [[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]]. With Reilly added to the first team in [[1947–48 in Scottish football|1947–48]], Hibs won the [[list of Scottish football champions|Scottish league championship]] for the first time since 1903. This was achieved despite the death of team manager [[Willie McCartney]] in January 1948. McCartney was succeeded by [[Hugh Shaw (footballer, born 1896)|Hugh Shaw]], who added Johnstone to the first team during 1948. Hibs finished third in the league in [[1948–49 in Scottish football|1948–49]]. In a [[Exhibition game|friendly match]] against [[Nithsdale Wanderers F.C.|Nithsdale Wanderers]] on 21 April 1949, Hibs included all of the famous five players in the same team for the first time. They then made their collective competitive debut on 15 October 1949, in a 2–0 win against [[Queen of the South F.C.|Queen of the South]].{{cite web |url=https://www.qosfc.com/History |title=Club History |publisher=Queen of the South FC |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110508013726/http://www.qosfc.com/history |date=13 September 2009 |archive-date=8 May 2011 |access-date=2 May 2017}} They improved on their season from the year before, by finishing second in the league to Rangers by one point. [[1950–51 in Scottish football|1950–51]] was the high point of the Famous Five era. With other internationalists such as [[Tommy Younger]] and [[Bobby Combe]], Hibs won the league by 10 points (when two points were awarded for each win). They reached the [[1950 Scottish League Cup final]]. Turnbull had scored a hattrick in the semi-final but was unavailable for the final. [[Jimmy Bradley]] started at left wing with Ormond moved to inside left. Motherwell beat them 3–0. Hibs retained the league championship in [[1951–52 in Scottish football|1951–52]], this time winning by four points. Hibs were narrowly denied a third consecutive title in [[1952–53 in Scottish football|1952–53]] on the last day of the season. A late Rangers equaliser against Queen of the South took the title to Ibrox on [[Goal difference#Goal difference v. goal average|goal average]]. The Famous Five forward line remained in place until March 1955, when Johnstone was sold to [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]]. {{See also|Hibernian F.C. in European football|1955–56 European Cup}} Despite only finishing fifth in the Scottish League in 1955, Hibs were invited to participate in the first season of the [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]], which was not strictly based on league positions at that time. Eighteen clubs who were thought would generate interest across Europe and who also had the [[floodlight]]s necessary to play games at night, were invited to participate.{{Cite news|last=Wilson |first=Richard |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/article545013.ece |title=European Union |work=The Sunday Times|publisher=News International |date=17 July 2005 |access-date=4 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629123237/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/article545013.ece |archive-date=29 June 2011}} Floodlights had been used at [[Easter Road]] for the first time in a [[Exhibition game|friendly match]] against Hearts on 18 October 1954.{{Cite web |url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/19541018.html |title=Mon 18 Oct 1954 |publisher=London Hearts Supporters' Club |work=Londonhearts.com |access-date=22 February 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081201193027/http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/19541018.html |archive-date=1 December 2008 |df=dmy-all }} Hibs became the first British club in Europe because the [[English Football League]] secretary [[Alan Hardaker]] persuaded [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]], the [[List of English football champions|English champions]], not to enter.{{Cite news|author-link=Brian Glanville |last=Glanville |first=Brian |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/european_football/article385542.ece |title=The great Chelsea surrender |work=The Times |date=27 April 2005 |access-date=4 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110811183830/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/european_football/article385542.ece |archive-date=11 August 2011}} Hibs played their first match against [[Rot-Weiss Essen]], winning 4–0 in the [[Georg-Melches-Stadion]] and drawing 1–1 at Easter Road. They defeated [[Djurgårdens IF Fotboll|Djurgårdens IF]] to reach the semi-final, but in that clash they were defeated 3–0 on [[Two-legged tie|aggregate]] by [[Stade de Reims]], who had the famous [[France national football team|France international]] player [[Raymond Kopa]] in their side. Reims lost 4–3 to [[Real Madrid CF|Real Madrid]] in the [[1956 European Cup Final|final]]. ===Turnbull's Tornadoes (1960–1989)=== Hibs frequently participated in the [[Inter-Cities Fairs Cup|Fairs Cup]] during the 1960s, winning matches against [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]]{{Cite news |last=Leslie |first=Colin |url=http://sport.scotsman.com/hibernianfc/Kinloch-still-treasures-shot-at.4182599.jp |title=Kinloch still treasures shot at glory |work=The Scotsman |publisher=Johnston Press |date=13 June 2008 |access-date=22 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081226003451/http://sport.scotsman.com/hibernianfc/Kinloch-still-treasures-shot-at.4182599.jp |archive-date=26 December 2008 |url-status=live }} and [[SSC Napoli|Napoli]].{{Cite web|url=http://sport.scotsman.com/hibernianfc/Classic-Match-Hibs-5-.3907874.jp|title=Classic Match: Hibs 5–0 Napoli, 29 November 1967|date=24 March 2008|publisher=Johnston Press|work=The Scotsman|access-date=23 February 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081226000044/http://sport.scotsman.com/hibernianfc/Classic-Match-Hibs-5-.3907874.jp|archive-date=26 December 2008|url-status=live}} However, the club achieved little domestically until former player [[Eddie Turnbull]] was persuaded to return to Easter Road as [[manager (association football)|manager]] in 1971. The team, popularly known as ''Turnbull's Tornadoes'', finished second in the league in 1974 and 1975 and won the [[Scottish League Cup|League Cup]] in 1972. The club also won the [[Drybrough Cup]] in 1972 and 1973, and recorded a 7–0 win over [[Edinburgh derby]] rivals Hearts at [[Tynecastle Park|Tynecastle]] on 1 January 1973. Performances went into decline after the mid-1970s, as Hibs were replaced by the [[New Firm (Scotland)|New Firm]] of [[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]] and [[Dundee United F.C.|Dundee United]] as the main challengers to the [[Old Firm]]. Turnbull resigned as manager and Hibs were [[promotion and relegation|relegated]], for the second time in their history, in 1980. They were immediately [[promotion and relegation|promoted]] back to the [[Scottish Premier Division]] in 1981, but the club struggled during the 1980s, failing to qualify for European competition until 1989. ===1990s: Attempted takeover by Hearts=== After mismanagement during the late 1980s, Hibs were on the brink of financial ruin in 1990.{{Cite web |last=Murray |first=Scott |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2001/may/03/sport.comment |title=Merger memories |work=The Guardian |date=3 May 2001 |access-date=22 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131002152452/http://www.theguardian.com/football/2001/may/03/sport.comment |archive-date=2 October 2013 |url-status=live }} [[Wallace Mercer]], the chairman of Hearts, proposed a merger of the two clubs, but the Hibs fans believed that the proposal was more like a [[hostile takeover]].{{Cite news|url=http://living.scotsman.com/theproclaimers/Family-and-football.2650156.jp |title=Family and football |work=The Scotsman |publisher=Johnston Press |date=9 August 2005 |access-date=22 February 2010 |last=Bowditch |first=Gillian}} They formed the ''Hands off Hibs'' group to campaign for the continued existence of the club.{{cite news |url=https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/hibs/creative-accountancy-how-jim-mclean-and-others-were-unlikely-saviours-hibs-wallace-mercer-circled-2873914 |title='Creative accountancy': How Jim McLean - and others - were unlikely saviours of Hibs as Wallace Mercer circled |newspaper=The Scotsman |date=4 June 2020 |access-date=5 June 2020 |first=Alan |last=Pattullo |archive-date=4 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200604215457/https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/hibs/creative-accountancy-how-jim-mclean-and-others-were-unlikely-saviours-hibs-wallace-mercer-circled-2873914 |url-status=live }} This succeeded when a prominent local businessman, [[Kwik Fit]] owner Sir [[Tom Farmer]], acquired a controlling interest in Hibs. derby|city rivals]] at Hampden Park in the 151 year history of the fixture. ==Colours and badge== {{Commons|Hibernian F.C. kits}} Green and white have been Hibernian's colours since the club's foundation in 1875. The club has developed a distinct visual identity around its traditional green shirts with contrasting white sleeves, usually accompanied by white shorts and green socks. The original kit was white with an [[Celtic harp|Irish harp]] on the chest, before Hibernian adopted green and white hoops in 1876.{{cite news |last=McPartlin |first=Patrick |title=Harp, crown, Saturn, and heritage: The history of the four Hibs club crests |url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/nostalgia/harp-crown-saturn-and-heritage-the-history-of-the-four-hibs-club-crests-3180758 |work=Edinburgh Evening News |date=26 March 2021}} This early design has been described as an inspiration for [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]]'s now-famous hooped strip, introduced in 1903.{{cite news |last1=Turner |first1=Georgina |last2=Dart |first2=James |title=Nicking the shirts off their backs |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2005/nov/23/theknowledge.sport |work=The Guardian |date=23 November 2005}} Hibs subsequently switched to plain green shirts before finally adopting white sleeves in 1938, following the example set by [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]].{{cite news |last=Greechan |first=John |title=Hibs stars don stunning retro jersey - 'Celtic' hoops reclaimed for Dundee United in 150th celebration |url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/football/hibs/hibs-hoops-celtic-retro-jersey-150th-anniversary-5316196 |work=Edinburgh Evening News |date=13 September 2025}} In 1977, Hibernian became the first British top-flight club to display shirt sponsorship, featuring the name of sportswear manufacturer [[Bukta]]. Television broadcasters initially refused to show matches involving sponsored shirts, prompting the introduction of an alternative purple-and-white kit. Purple subsequently became a recurring colour for the club's change strips, including several notable designs during the 1990s.{{cite web |title=Hibernian |url=https://www.historicalkits.co.uk/Scottish_Football_League/Hibernian/hibernian.htm |website=Historical Football Kits |access-date=28 October 2026}} To celebrate its 150th anniversary in 2025, Hibernian released a limited-edition white heritage shirt inspired by its original 1875 kit, alongside a green-and-white hooped design recreating the club's early colours. The latter was worn for a special match against [[Dundee United F.C.|Dundee United]] at [[Easter Road]] in September 2025.{{cite web |title=Hibernian 2025 Joma 1875 Heritage Top |url=https://www.footballshirtculture.com/new-kits/hibernian-2025-joma-1875-heritage-top.html |website=Football Shirt Culture |date=6 August 2025}}{{cite news |last=Greechan |first=John |title=Hibs stars don stunning retro jersey - 'Celtic' hoops reclaimed for Dundee United in 150th celebration |url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/football/hibs/hibs-hoops-celtic-retro-jersey-150th-anniversary-5316196 |work=Edinburgh Evening News |date=13 September 2025}} The current club badge, introduced in 2000, brings together three symbols of Hibernian's heritage: the Irish harp representing its origins, a ship symbolising the [[Port of Leith]], and a castle representing [[Edinburgh]].{{cite news |last=McPartlin |first=Patrick |title=Harp, crown, Saturn, and heritage: The history of the four Hibs club crests |url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/nostalgia/harp-crown-saturn-and-heritage-the-history-of-the-four-hibs-club-crests-3180758 |work=Edinburgh Evening News |date=26 March 2021}} The harp is also central to a longstanding supporters' legend involving a so-called "gypsy curse", said to have been placed on the club after a harp emblem was removed from Easter Road during renovations in the 1950s.{{cite news |last=Bogue |first=Declan |title=Sunshine on Leith: The Irish origins of Hibernian FC, as they celebrate 150 years |url=https://www.the42.ie/hibernian-150-years-irish-roots-6791524-Aug2025/ |work=The42 |date=August 2025}} According to the legend, Hibernian would not win another [[Scottish Cup]] until the harp was restored. In 2015, a harp mosaic and large club crests were reinstated at the stadium. Shield|Festival Cup|Rosebery Charity Cup|Wilson Cup (football)}} Hibernian shares a rivalry with fellow Edinburgh club [[Heart of Midlothian F.C.|Heart of Midlothian]], with whom they contest the [[Edinburgh derby]], one of the oldest rivalries in world football. The fixture dates to Christmas Day 1875, when the clubs first met at [[The Meadows, Edinburgh|The Meadows]] in Hibernian's first recorded match.{{cite web |title=Hearts and Hibs Reveal Commemorative Plaque in the Meadows |url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/blogs/news/hearts-and-hibs-reveal-commemorative-plaque-in-the-meadows |website=Heart of Midlothian F.C. |date=9 January 2026 |access-date=28 October 2026}} The clubs are traditionally associated with different parts of Edinburgh, Hibernian with [[Leith]] and Heart of Midlothian with [[Gorgie]]. Football journalist [[Graham Spiers]] has described the derby as "one of the jewels of the Scottish game". The clubs have contested two [[Scottish Cup]] finals, in [[1896 Scottish Cup final|1896]] and [[2012 Scottish Cup final|2012]], both won by Heart of Midlothian. The 1896 final, held in Edinburgh, remains the only Scottish Cup final played outside [[Glasgow]].{{cite web |title=Hearts and Hibernian: the Edinburgh derby |url=https://scottishfootballhistory.scot/derbies/edinburgh/ |website=Scottish Football History |access-date=28 October 2026}} Although Heart of Midlothian hold the better overall head-to-head record, Hibernian achieved the largest victory in a competitive derby, winning 7–0 at [[Tynecastle Park|Tynecastle]] on New Year's Day 1973.{{cite web |title=Hearts vs Hibs Competitive Games Only |url=https://www.londonhearts.com/scores/misc/hibscomp.htm |website=London Hearts |access-date=28 October 2026}} The rivalry was further intensified by an unsuccessful 1990 takeover bid for Hibernian by Heart of Midlothian chairman [[Wallace Mercer]], which prompted the "Hands Off Hibs" campaign.{{cite journal |last1=Kelly |first1=John |last2=Bairner |first2=Alan |title=The 'talk o' the toon'? An examination of the Heart of Midlothian and Hibernian football rivalry in Edinburgh, Scotland |journal=Soccer & Society |year=2018 |volume=19 |issue=5–6 |pages=657–672 |doi=10.1080/14660970.2017.1399610}} Although historically associated with religious and ethnic divisions, the modern rivalry is shaped more by geography, local identity and perceptions of social class than by sectarianism.{{cite journal |last1=Kelly |first1=John |last2=Bairner |first2=Alan |title=The 'talk o' the toon'? An examination of the Heart of Midlothian and Hibernian football rivalry in Edinburgh, Scotland |journal=Soccer & Society |year=2018 |volume=19 |issue=5–6 |pages=657–672 |doi=10.1080/14660970.2017.1399610}} ==Supporters== [[File:Easter Road Block Seven.jpg|thumb|Block Seven during an [[Edinburgh derby]] match on 26 April 2026.|left]] Hibernian have a longstanding supporter base with strong roots in [[Leith]], north and eastern [[Edinburgh]], as well as followings across the [[Lothians]], [[Fife]] and [[Scottish Borders]].{{cite report |last1=Jarvie |first1=Grant |last2=Barrett |first2=Jake |last3=Widdop |first3=Paul |title=2022 Hibernian Fan Engagement Research Report |publisher=University of Edinburgh |date=2022 |url=https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/2022-hibernian-fan-engagement-research-report/ |access-date=28 October 2026}} Hibernian have historically attracted some of the largest crowds in Scottish football. A [[1947–48 Scottish Cup|Scottish Cup semi-final]] against [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] in March 1948 attracted more than 143,000 spectators to [[Hampden Park]], a record attendance for a Scottish Cup match outside the final.{{cite news |title=Scotland's record football attendances |url=https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/scotlands-record-football-attendances-1449406 |work=The Scotsman |access-date=28 October 2026}} The club regularly averaged more than 20,000 spectators in the years following the Second World War, averaging a high of 31,567 during the [[1951–52 in Scottish football|1951–52 season]].{{cite web |title=Average Home League Game Attendances |url=https://www.fitbastats.com/hibs/club_records_league_attendance.php |website=FitbaStats |access-date=28 October 2026}} Following the redevelopment of [[Easter Road]] into an [[all-seater stadium]], average home league attendances reached 18,510 in [[2025–26 Hibernian F.C. season|2025–26]]. During the 1980s and 1990s, a minority of Hibernian's supporters became associated with the [[Capital City Service]] (CCS), one of Britain's most prominent football [[Casual (subculture)|casual]] groups.{{cite news |last=Smith |first=Mark |title=Hibs thugs boast of violence on internet |work=Edinburgh Evening News |date=10 January 2003 |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090530021335/http://news.scotsman.com/footballhooligans/Hibs-thugs-boast-of-violence.2392263.jp |access-date=28 October 2026}} The group has been the subject of several books, including Derek Dykes' ''These Colours Don't Run'' (2007) and Andy Blance's ''Hibs Boy'' (2010).{{cite book |last=Dykes |first=Derek |title=These Colours Don't Run: Inside the Hibs Capital City Service |publisher=Fort Publishing |year=2007 |isbn=9781905769070}}{{cite book |last=Blance |first=Andy |title=Hibs Boy: The Life and Violent Times of Scotland's Most Notorious Football Hooligan |publisher=Fort Publishing |year=2010 |isbn=9781905769193}} The club's modern [[Ultras|ultras]] group, Block Seven, was established in 2021 and has become known for organised vocal support, banners and large-scale [[Tifo|tifo displays]] at Easter Road and away matches.{{cite web |title=Get To Know: Block Seven |url=https://www.hibernianfc.co.uk/news/2022/october/20/Get-To-Know-Block-Seven/ |website=Hibernian FC |date=20 October 2022 |access-date=28 October 2026}} Supporters played a significant role in the 1990 [[#1990s: Attempted takeover by Hearts|Hands Off Hibs]] campaign, which opposed a proposed takeover of Hibernian by Wallace Mercer, chairman of Heart of Midlothian. The supporter-owned organisation Hibernian Supporters (HSL), established in 2015, has since invested more than £3 million in the club and holds approximately 7% of its shares on behalf of its members.{{cite web |title=About Us |url=https://hiberniansupporters.co.uk/about/ |website=Hibernian Supporters |access-date=28 October 2026}} ===Sunshine on Leith=== One of Hibernian's most celebrated traditions is the supporters' singing of ''[[Sunshine on Leith (song)|Sunshine on Leith]]'', the 1988 song by Scottish duo [[the Proclaimers]]. The song became closely associated with the club during the 1990s and is traditionally sung following significant victories at Easter Road and in cup finals.{{cite news |title=How Hands Off Hibs helped Sunshine on Leith become an Easter Road anthem |url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/heritage-and-retro/retro/how-hands-off-hibs-helped-sunshine-on-leith-become-an-easter-road-anthem-2875873 |work=Edinburgh Evening News |access-date=28 October 2026}} Its most famous rendition followed Hibernian's 3–2 victory over Rangers in the [[2016 Scottish Cup final]], ending the club's 114-year wait to lift the trophy. The emotional scenes at Hampden Park attracted widespread acclaim, with former Manchester United manager [[Alex Ferguson|Sir Alex Ferguson]] declaring: "I don't think there's a better football celebration ever in the game."{{cite news |title=Alex Ferguson: No better celebration than Hibs' Sunshine on Leith |url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/football/alex-ferguson-no-better-celebration-than-hibs-sunshine-on-leith-587763 |work=Edinburgh Evening News |access-date=28 October 2026}} A recording of the supporters' singing had attracted approximately 3.8 million views on [[YouTube]] by October 2026.{{cite web |title=Tears!
